verdict.justification: A is the stronger workflow blueprint because it preserves the required approvals while making post-nomination changes faster through modular pricing and parallel, tiered sign-offs. Its explicit rule that every price change requires “Finance Controller, Program Manager and Purchase” corrects a material weakness in B, where Class A changes leave the PM merely “informed.” A also requires ER, Quality and Purchase approval of every TRSO version, whereas B permits acknowledgment rather than sign-off for minor changes. Both deliverables provide useful modular quotation models and platform requirements, but A adds stronger implementation controls, including quotation reconciliation, cumulative-change monitoring and explicit precedence when multiple change classes apply. A’s provisional tooling authorization also requires the relevant financial and program approvals, while B leaves authorization primarily with Purchase and only specifies that Finance sets the cap and expiry. A is substantially more verbose and less well suited to the requested 2–3-page executive format, but its stronger governance and more executable change-control rules outweigh that drawback.

decisive_issues.issue: Minor price changes omit the Program Manager's required approval.
decisive_issues.quote: Purchase + Finance controller (delegated). Quality and ER acknowledge; PM informed.

decisive_issues.issue: The minor-change route substitutes acknowledgment for required TRSO sign-offs.

decisive_issues.issue: Adds cumulative-change safeguards against splitting changes to evade scrutiny.
decisive_issues.quote: Once the cumulative impact passes 10%, every further CR is classed C.

decisive_issues.issue: Provisional tooling authorization does not explicitly require PM approval or a complete financial approval gate.
decisive_issues.quote: Purchase may issue a capped, time-limited Letter of Authority so the supplier starts development/tooling while pricing closes. Cap and expiry set by Finance
